questions.q: For \( (x^{2} - x)y''+y'-y=0 \), the point \( x=0 \) is:
choices: a point where no solution exists
a point where every solution vanishes
questions.answer: Dividing by \( x^{2} - x \) gives \( y''+P(x)y'+Q(x)y=0 \). The leading coefficient vanishes at \( x=0 \), so \( P,Q \) are not analytic there: it is a singular point.

questions.q: Near \( x_0=0 \), the power series solutions of \( (x + 4)y''+xy'+y=0 \) are guaranteed to converge at least for \( |x-x_0|<R \) with \( R= \)
questions.answer: The singular points are the zeros of \( x + 4 \): \( -4 \) (complex ones count). The nearest is at distance \( 4 \) from \( 0 \).

questions.q: Consider the differential equation \( y'' - xy = 0 \). The point \( x=0 \) is an ordinary point. If we assume a power series solution of the form \( y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n \), find the recurrence relation for the coefficients \( c_n \).
questions.answer:
We are given the differential equation \( y'' - xy = 0 \) and assume a power series solution of the form \( y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n \). 
ewline Differentiating twice with respect to \( x \), we get: \( y'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n c_n x^{n-1} \) and \( y''(x) = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n(n-1) c_n x^{n-2} \). 
ewline Substituting these into the differential equation: \( \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n(n-1) c_n x^{n-2} - x \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n = 0 \). 
ewline We can rewrite the second term as \( \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n+1} \). To combine the series, we need the powers of \( x \) to be the same. Let \( k = n-2 \) in the first series, so \( n = k+2 \). When \( n=2, k=0 \). The first series becomes \( \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (k+2)(k+1) c_{k+2} x^k \). 
ewline Let \( k = n+1 \) in the second series, so \( n = k-1 \). When \( n=0, k=1 \). The second series becomes \( \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} c_{k-1} x^k \). 
ewline So the equation is \( \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (k+2)(k+1) c_{k+2} x^k - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} c_{k-1} x^k = 0 \). 
ewline We can separate the \( k=0 \) term from the first sum: \( 2(1)c_2 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (k+2)(k+1) c_{k+2} x^k - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} c_{k-1} x^k = 0 \). 
ewline For this equation to hold for all \( x \), the coefficients of each power of \( x \) must be zero. 
ewline For \( k=0 \): \( 2c_2 = 0 \) implies \( c_2 = 0 \). 
ewline For \( k \geq 1 \): \( (k+2)(k+1) c_{k+2} - c_{k-1} = 0 \). 
ewline Thus, the recurrence relation is \( c_{k+2} =  rac{c_{k-1}}{(k+2)(k+1)} \) for \( k \geq 1 \). Replacing \( k \) with \( n \), we get \( c_{n+2} =  rac{c_{n-1}}{(n+2)(n+1)} \) for \( n \geq 1 \).

questions.q: The Laplace transform of \( h(u) = 190e^{20u} \) is \( k(s) = \dfrac{190}{s - 20} \) for \( s > 20 \). Determine the evaluated transform \( k(21) \).
questions.answer: Substituting \( s = 21 \) gives \( \frac{190}{21 - 20} = 190 \).

questions.q: Consider the differential equation \(y'' - xy = 0\). We are looking for a power series solution of the form \(y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n\) around the ordinary point \(x=0\). Find the coefficient \(a_2\) in terms of \(a_0\) and \(a_1\).
questions.answer:
We assume a power series solution of the form \(y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n\). Then \(y'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n a_n x^{n-1}\) and \(y''(x) = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n(n-1) a_n x^{n-2}\).
Substituting these into the differential equation \(y'' - xy = 0\), we get:
\(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n(n-1) a_n x^{n-2} - x \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n = 0\)
\(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n(n-1) a_n x^{n-2} - \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^{n+1} = 0\).
To compare coefficients, we need the powers of \(x\) to be the same. Let \(k = n-2\) in the first sum, so \(n = k+2\). When \(n=2\), \(k=0\). Let \(k = n+1\) in the second sum, so \(n = k-1\). When \(n=0\), \(k=1\).
\(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (k+2)(k+1) a_{k+2} x^k - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_{k-1} x^k = 0\).
We can split off the \(k=0\) term from the first sum:
\(2(1)a_2 x^0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (k+2)(k+1) a_{k+2} x^k - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_{k-1} x^k = 0\).
\(2a_2 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [(k+2)(k+1) a_{k+2} - a_{k-1}] x^k = 0\).
For this equation to hold for all \(x\), the coefficients of each power of \(x\) must be zero.
For the constant term (\(x^0\)), we have \(2a_2 = 0\), which implies \(a_2 = 0\).
For \(k \geq 1\), we have the recurrence relation \((k+2)(k+1) a_{k+2} - a_{k-1} = 0\), or \(a_{k+2} = \frac{a_{k-1}}{(k+2)(k+1)}\).
